On Agentic Manipulation Policies

Journal: ol
Chen Chen†    Omid Bagherieh†    Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji†    Jesse T. Gonzalez†    Negin Heravi†    Fahad Islam†    Xueting Li†    Jean-Baptiste Regli†    Kejia Ren†    Petr Švec†    David J. Yoon†    Matthias Müller    Vladlen Koltun Affiliation: Apple Affiliation: †These authors contributed equally to this work.
Abstract

Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

1 Introduction

In nature, manipulation draws on general intelligence. Animals can recruit their memory, reasoning, and problem-solving faculties when interacting with objects, with cognitive processes continuing to shape action as it unfolds [1, 2, 3]. In robotics, much recent work has focused on models specialized for robot control, including vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs), trained or fine-tuned on robot demonstrations [4, 5].

Generalist AI models have also been applied to manipulation, often through skill orchestration or offline program synthesis. In the first setting (skill orchestration), the model selects and sequences low-level skills such as grasping and placing [6, 7, 8]. It can revise the plan as new observations arrive, but the available skills limit the generalist model’s control authority and the granularity at which it can command the manipulator. Since the generalist model’s interactions with the world are mediated by the provided skills, it is constrained by the skills’ limitations. In the second setting (offline program synthesis, sometimes known as ‘code-as-policies’), the model writes a control program before execution [9, 10, 11, 12]. The program can incorporate perception and feedback, but the generalist model is not in the loop and cannot reconsider the overall control strategy as the task unfolds.

A key obstacle to direct manipulation has been the limited spatial cognition of generalist frontier models [13]. However, spatial cognition has been advancing [14, 15], with recent models demonstrating convincing spatial planning, sensorimotor coordination, and embodied fluid intelligence [16, 17]. These advances make a third approach increasingly viable: the generalist model remains in the control loop and commands the manipulator directly, revising its actions as the task unfolds [18, 19, 20, 21]. We refer to this category as Agentic Manipulation Policies (AMPs).

In this paper, we systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies across models and harness configurations. We present AMP1, a reference harness that provides visual observations, code execution, and direct control of manipulator motion. Paired with frontier models, AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results on the RoboLab-120 [22] and CaP-Gym [18] benchmarks. The agent succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, compared to 49 for FLUX 3 Action [23] and 30 for π0.5\pi_{0.5} [24], thus reducing the failure rate by 15x and 20x, respectively, relative to these WAM and VLA baselines. See Fig. 1 and the supplementary video for curated highlights.

We document emergent behaviors that arise as the agent brings its broader cognitive faculties to bear on manipulation. When a book lies flat on a table and cannot be grasped as is, the agent pushes it to the table edge to expose a graspable surface. When a target object is hidden, the agent moves occluding objects out of the way to find it. When a large fruit is too wide to grasp, the agent pins it against a heavier object, slides the gripper underneath, and lifts it like a forklift. Failed actions can themselves supply information: the agent infers an unseen shelf from a blocked motion and changes its grasp and approach. On the real robot, the agent diagnoses camera calibration errors from discrepancies between commanded and observed motion, then compensates for them in subsequent actions. None of these behaviors are specified in the prompt or supplied as skills in the harness. The generalist model develops them within each episode by reasoning about geometry, contact, and the consequences of its own actions.

We also investigate few-shot and continual learning from the agent’s own experience. We equip AMP1 with a persistent memory, allowing the agent to record useful observations, strategies, and code after reflecting on its successes and failures. Experience accumulates in this memory bank, while the model’s weights remain fixed. No expert demonstrations or gradient updates are required. We evaluate this approach on the 42 bimanual manipulation tasks of RoboDojo [25]. Practicing individual tasks raises the success rate on unseen layouts from 26.4% to 84.1%, above all entries on the benchmark’s leaderboard. We also test whether the agent can accumulate knowledge across tasks via continual learning. In this setting, the agent attempts each task once, in sequence, and updates its memory representation in the course of this continual deployment. A single pass through the tasks more than doubles the success rate, to 57.6%. Learning transfers to tasks not yet attempted without erasing gains on tasks already encountered. Experience improves efficiency as well: an agent with memory uses about 35% fewer model calls in comparison to zero-shot deployment.

We conduct controlled experiments to isolate the effects of the model, its reasoning effort, and the harness’s perception and motion interfaces. The choice of model has the largest effect. For example, AMP1’s success rate on RoboLab-120 is 82.8% with Opus 5.5, 51.6% with Haiku 5.5, and 35.2% with Opus 4.5. More reasoning helps all evaluated models. The value of additional harness support depends on the model. Weaker models are helped by assistive grasping and placing routines, while stronger models perform best without these routines. Stronger models also cope better with missing sensory information. With the AMP1 harness, Opus 5.5 achieves a success rate of 82.8% with full sensory input, 81.1% without direct depth input, and 75.8% without depth or camera calibration. While the overall success rate does not suffer much, sensory impairment takes a toll on efficiency. The agent routes around limited sensory input by reconstructing 3D points via triangulation across views and, when needed, estimates camera calibration from images taken at known gripper poses. The mean number of model calls per episode rises from 34.8 with full sensory input to 46.3 without direct depth input and 53.5 without depth or camera calibration. A weaker model cannot compensate for impoverished perception: the success rate of AMP1 with Haiku 5.5 on RoboLab-120 collapses from 51.6% with full sensory input to 10.7% without depth or camera calibration. Our experiments also indicate that replacing visual input with textual descriptions has a sharply detrimental effect, for example cutting the success rate of AMP1 with Opus 5.5 from 82.8% to 36.8%; this contrasts with prior work, which recommended replacing visual input with textual descriptions [18].

Our results point to agentic manipulation policies as a promising foundation for generalist manipulation. AMPs are not yet practical, as the robot spends much of each episode waiting for the model to reason. But neither are the alternatives: the strongest VLA and WAM entries on the RoboLab-120 leaderboard at the time of writing succeed in 49.2% and 42.9% of the episodes, respectively, in contrast to AMP1’s 85.6%. A policy that fails every other task is not practical, however quickly it does so. We see a more promising path in making capable policies fast. Recent studies estimate that the cost of a given capability level has fallen by roughly an order of magnitude per year [26, 27]. A harness could further reduce waiting by reusing generated code, running feedback loops locally [9, 28, 29], and planning the next motion while the current one executes [30]. AMP experience could also be used to synthesize closed-loop onboard controllers [29] or train compact models through distillation [11, 31]. Our analysis suggests that agentic manipulation policies are substantially more general and robust than alternative paradigms, opening the way to broad deployment of generalist manipulation capabilities across hardware embodiments and application domains.

2 Results

2A AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results

2A.1 Benchmarks

We chose four simulation benchmarks that facilitate comprehensive quantitative evaluation of AMP1 against the most effective learned policies and other agents (Fig. 2A). RoboLab-120 comprises 120 manipulation tasks specified in natural language [22]. The tasks span visual, relational, and procedural competencies; each is posed with default, vague, and specific instructions. The other three benchmarks are suites of CaP-Gym [18]: LIBERO-PRO perturbs object positions and instructions to test whether a policy generalizes beyond familiar scenes [32]; robosuite has five unimanual and two bimanual tasks [33]; and two tasks from BEHAVIOR-1K that require mobile manipulation in a simulated home [34]. We run 10 episodes per task on RoboLab-120 (3,600 in total across the default, vague, and specific instruction conditions), 50 on LIBERO-PRO (3,000 in total), 100 on robosuite (700), and 25 on BEHAVIOR-1K (50). The AMP1 harness is the same on all four benchmarks; only the robot description and camera configuration change. AMP1 solves every episode zero-shot: in a single attempt, without demonstrations, training, or practice rollouts.

On RoboLab-120, AMP1 paired with Gemini 4 Argon succeeds in 85.6% of episodes (95% confidence interval, 83.5 to 87.5%), and in 82.8% when paired with Opus 5.5 (95% CI, 80.6 to 84.9%) – the highest success rates reported on the benchmark (Fig. 2B). The strongest entry on the RoboLab-120 public leaderboard at the time of writing is also an agent: SenseNova-RoboRSI, which is based on GPT-6 Astra [35]; it has a 57.1% success rate. The strongest learned policy on the leaderboard, Lakeside, has a 51.0% success rate, and the strongest VLA and WAM entries are at 49.2% and 42.9%, respectively. Astranomy, an agentic manipulation policy evaluated outside the leaderboard, reaches 74.8% with GPT-6 Astra [21]. Astranomy also reported a 25.3% success rate with Opus 5.5 on a 30-task subset of RoboLab; this contrasts with the 82.8% success rate achieved by AMP1 with Opus 5.5 on the full RoboLab-120.

AMP1 is robust across instruction conditions. In RoboLab’s ‘vague’ and ‘specific’ instruction conditions, AMP1 succeeds in 84.0% and 87.1% of episodes with Gemini 4 Argon, and in 79.8% and 82.8% of episodes with Opus 5.5, respectively. The success rate thus varies by about three points across the three conditions (Supplementary Section S5 and Fig. S9). Specialist policies are far more brittle: with vague instructions, FLUX 3 Action [23] falls from 42.9% to 28.4% and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [24] from 28.0% to 15.2%. (Since the RoboLab-120 leaderboard does not report FLUX 3 Action performance under the ‘vague’ and ‘specific’ conditions, we evaluated it ourselves on these conditions using its publicly released checkpoint.)

AMP1’s success rate on RoboLab-120 approaches saturation, with the remaining failures bounded largely by benchmark artifacts rather than policy errors (Supplementary Materials, Sec. S6, and Fig. S10). Across the 1,200 trials in the ‘default’ instruction condition, 121 of the 173 unsuccessful episodes with Gemini 4 Argon and 135 of the 206 unsuccessful episodes with Opus 5.5 can be traced to issues with the benchmark setup: either the object’s geometry or mass defeats a standard parallel-jaw grasp (77 and 101 episodes, respectively) or a flaky verifier rejects an end state that satisfies the instruction (44 and 34 episodes). Only two tasks fail all 10 trials for both models; the remaining affected tasks still succeed in about half of their trials when a placement happens to satisfy the verifier’s geometric check or when AMP1 improvises a non-standard grasp (Sec. 2B). Across the 95 tasks that do not suffer from these benchmark artifacts, AMP1 with Gemini 4 Argon succeeds in 96.2% of episodes (914 of 950).

On CaP-Gym, the strongest agent baselines – HarnessPAI [12], ASPIRE [36], and Harness VLA [37] – all involve improving a program, a skill library, or a memory representation over rollouts of the evaluated tasks and are thus not zero-shot. In contrast, AMP1 solves every episode zero-shot, using the same harness in CaP-Gym as in RoboLab (Fig. 2C–E).

On the LIBERO-PRO subset of CaP-Gym, AMP1 with Gemini 4 Argon succeeds in 95.2% of episodes, against 18.2% for CaP-Agent0 [18], the only other zero-shot agent, and 34.9% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}, a fine-tuned VLA [24]. Only HarnessPAI [12], which evolves its program on seeds that lie inside the evaluation, scores higher (96.5%). Its lead comes entirely from LIBERO-Goal (94.6% and 97.8% against 81.4% and 91.4% under swap and task perturbations, respectively), while AMP1 is ahead on LIBERO-Object and LIBERO-Spatial. In almost all of the unsuccessful LIBERO-Goal episodes, AMP1 ended the episode believing it had succeeded. The instructions do not say what LIBERO checks, such as which side of the stove counts as its front or how far a drawer must open, and a human review of the episodes marked as failures suggests that AMP1 interpreted the instructions in a way that is consistent with human interpretation but inconsistent with the verifier implemented by the benchmark. HarnessPAI utilizes a VLA that was fine-tuned on LIBERO demonstrations that succeed according to the implemented verifier, thus leaking the verifier’s implementation into the training data.

On the robosuite subset of CaP-Gym, AMP1 paired with Gemini 4 Argon succeeds in all 700 episodes, including the two tasks that require coordinating two arms, against 96.3% for HarnessPAI [12] and 82.6% for programs written and debugged by human experts [18]. On the two BEHAVIOR-1K tasks in CaP-Gym, AMP1 succeeds in 48 of 50 episodes (96%), against 64% for CaP-Agent0 and 54% for human-written programs [18]; only ASPIRE [36], which evolves its programs over rollouts of the same task (and is thus not zero-shot), succeeds in every episode.

2A.2 Real-world trials

AMP1’s strong performance on benchmarks is matched in zero-shot trials on real-world hardware. We provide quantitative and qualitative results from diverse real-world manipulation tasks. All real-world experiments were conducted using a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm equipped with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper and a three-camera vision system similar to DROID [38] (left and right shoulder views, plus a wrist-mounted camera). The AMP1 harness was paired with Claude Opus 5.5 at high reasoning effort. The results are reported in Table 1.

We designed 12 challenging short- and long-horizon manipulation tasks and evaluated AMP1 against leading VLA and WAM policies, π0.5\pi_{0.5} and FLUX 3 Action [24, 23]. The tasks cover a broad range of capabilities, including prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation, spatial and temporal reasoning, semantic grounding, and object exclusion. We include both single- and multi-step tasks, the latter containing two or more subtasks. The results of the real-world trials are presented in Table 1. Further details of our experimental setup and evaluation protocols are provided in Sec. 4F. All tasks are illustrated in the Supplementary Materials (Fig. S2).

AMP1 matches or outperforms the baselines on all 12 tasks. It particularly excels in scenarios that require object identification in crowded settings or complex manipulation strategies, such as non-prehensile interaction. Overall, AMP1 achieves a 96.3% success rate, compared to 45.4% for FLUX and 27.8% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Baseline methods struggle to accurately identify target objects and frequently grasp incorrect objects, including those explicitly excluded by the task prompt. For example, when instructed to “Put all the tools except the hammer in the right bin”, both baselines still occasionally grasp the excluded object.

Most real-world struggles of AMP1 are caused by collision, mainly with the surface of the table, the walls of the bin, and self-collision. These collisions occur because the underlying motion planning is sensitive to camera calibration and relies on approximations including simplified robot geometry and unmodeled hardware such as camera mounts and cables. Collisions can trigger the Franka controller’s collision reflex, which interrupts motion when estimated external forces or torques exceed configured thresholds. The resulting error must be cleared before commanded motion can resume. We provide SDK functions through which the agent can query the arm’s state and request error recovery. Following successful recovery, the agent can replan and continue the task. With this functionality, AMP1 fails in only 4 out of 108 trials. (In two, some cubes fell outside the target plate during pouring. In the other two, a bowl rolled off the table.) Without these functions, our evaluation protocol terminates a trial when a robot controller error interrupts motion; in this condition, AMP1 succeeds in 94 of 108 trials (87.0%; Tab. S1).

A primary advantage of AMP1 is its capacity for dynamic error recovery and replanning as the task unfolds. For instance, for a task that requires moving a flipped bowl placed on top of a flat bin, where no initial feasible grasp exists, AMP1 recognizes that a direct grasp is infeasible and pushes the bowl to hang from the side of the bin where it can be grasped, thus combining non-prehensile and prehensile techniques (Fig. S3A). In contrast, baseline methods often continue pursuing hard or infeasible strategies (e.g., an intractable grasp) until the episode times out. Furthermore, for tasks that require complex semantic understanding, such as covering and uncovering multiple cubes with cups, the baseline methods perform inconsistent actions indicative of challenges with task comprehension. π0.5\pi_{0.5} is particularly prone to exhibiting indecisive behavior, repeatedly grasping and dropping a correctly identified target object without completing the placement.

A number of case studies, documented in Fig. 1 and the supplementary video, demonstrate that AMP1 can generalize zero-shot to even more complex tasks that require sequential dependency planning via interactive perception: manipulating the environment to uncover and subsequently manipulate hidden objects (Fig. 1A), devising effective tool-use strategies (Fig. 1B), reasoning through and physically executing a winning strategy in a game of chess followed by putting away the pieces (Fig. 1C), pushing or sliding to reveal occluded grasps (Fig. 1D), and manipulating articulated objects (Fig. 1E).

2B Emergent behaviors

Beyond aggregate task performance, we examine the manipulation strategies developed by AMP1 during execution. None of the behaviors described below was specified in the prompt or provided as a predefined skill in the harness. The agent develops these strategies while solving tasks, combining geometric reasoning, visual feedback, and physical interaction to construct higher-level manipulation skills. We highlight several examples, some of which are shown in Fig. 3 and the supplementary video.

Searching for hidden objects.

When the instructed object is not visible from any camera, AMP1 does not stop at what it sees. It reasons about which objects are large enough to hide the target, moves them aside one at a time, and looks again after each move until the target appears (Fig. 3A). The robotics literature calls this mechanical search [39], a form of interactive perception [40]: the agent acts to gain information, not only to make progress on the task.

Moving the goal instead of the object.

When an object cannot be grasped, AMP1 sometimes brings the goal to the object instead. In one task, “Put the bowl on the plate”, the bowl lay upside down on a bin, too wide for the gripper and with no edge the fingers could reach under (Fig. 3B). AMP1 instead grasped the plate by its rim and slid it up against the side of the bin, then pushed the bowl across the bin with the open gripper until it fell off the edge onto the plate. The bowl was never held: it reached its goal by non-prehensile manipulation alone.

Using objects as tools.

In some cases in which an object lies beyond the arm’s reach, AMP1 can use another item in the scene as a tool. It first establishes from inverse kinematics that the object is out of reach, and by how much. It then searches the scene for a tool long enough to cover that distance and reasons about how to use it to apply force, for example pulling rather than pushing so that the object moves toward the arm (Fig. 3C). Once the object is within reach, it sets the tool aside and grasps the object directly. None of this is described in the prompt, suggesting that AMP1 can at times improvise tool use from its understanding of geometry and contact. This strategy parallels tool selection in New Caledonian crows, which choose sticks long enough to retrieve otherwise inaccessible food [41], and has precedents in robotics [42].

Scooping objects too wide to grasp.

When an object, such as a large pomegranate, is wider than the gripper’s 85-mm stroke in every direction, AMP1 sometimes pins it against a heavier object so that it cannot roll or slide away (Fig. 3D). It then slides the open gripper beneath it and lifts it like a forklift to carry it to the goal. Like pushing an object to the table edge, this strategy exploits contact with the environment to achieve a grasp the gripper cannot achieve alone, a capability known as extrinsic dexterity [43].

Pushing to enable grasping.

When an object is too wide to grasp where it lies, AMP1 pushes it toward the edge of its supporting surface until part of it overhangs, giving the gripper a narrower part to hold (Fig. S3A). When objects stand too close together to grasp one at a time, it pushes them apart (Fig. S3B). In both cases, AMP1 treats the scene as something it can rearrange rather than a fixed input: when no grasp is feasible, it first acts to create one, a strategy known as pre-grasp manipulation [44].

Correcting calibration errors.

On the physical robot, camera calibration is imperfect, and the resulting errors in estimated poses can be too large for precise manipulation. When a motion misses its target, AMP1 compares where the gripper appears in the images with where it was commanded to go, attributes the offset to the calibration and corrects it (Fig. S3C). It then uses the corrected calibration for the rest of the episode. The same reasoning lets it calibrate the wrist camera from scratch when no calibration is given (Supplementary Materials, Sec. S4.1).

Gentle placement of long objects.

When placing a long object, AMP1 first rests one end on the surface, then lowers the other along an arc (Fig. S3D). This strategy uses surface contact to support the object during lowering, suggesting reasoning about contact and the physical consequences of the placement motion.

Reorienting objects by hooking and pivoting the gripper.

For objects lying on their side, AMP1 sometimes closes the gripper, inserts the closed fingers into the object’s opening, and uses them as a hook while moving the gripper along an arc until the object stands upright (Fig. S4A). For objects placed upside down, it first grasps an outer feature to tip the object onto its side, then hooks and pivots it.

Inferring environmental constraints from physical interaction.

In one task, AMP1 must place an object on a shelf whose top is not visible from any camera, so that part of the shelf is missing from its point cloud. Its first placement motion fails when the arm is blocked by this unseen geometry. From the gap between the commanded and reached end-effector poses, AMP1 infers that an upper shelf lies just outside its field of view, assumes it sits at the edge of the visible region to leave a safety margin, and adjusts its grasp and approach angle accordingly (Fig. S4B). AMP1 thus treats a failed action as a measurement, using physical interaction to recover information its cameras cannot provide. Together with its behavior in the wrist-camera setting (Sec. 2D.3), where it moves the arm back to see more of the scene, this suggests that AMP1 uses action as a source of information, not only as a means of changing the scene.

Mechanical interlocking grasps for heavy objects.

Through interaction with the environment, AMP1 discovers that friction-based grasps are brittle for heavy objects and prone to slippage. When the object’s geometry allows it, AMP1 switches to a mechanical interlocking grasp. For example, to lift a heavy drill, instead of grasping it from the top, it closes the fingers around the top of the handle, just below the drill’s head (Fig. S4C). Upon lifting, the head rests on the fingers, which yields an inherently stable grip that does not depend on friction.

Beyond these examples, we measured how often AMP1 composes the same building blocks across many tasks (Fig. 3E). We matched the code AMP1 executed and the intentions stated in its reasoning, in 1,200 RoboLab episodes, against a set of skill patterns, and report a pattern as a skill only if it recurs (a) in at least five episodes and (b) in at least two tasks; the first condition excludes rare improvisations and spurious matches, and the second excludes procedures that serve a single task. Because the harness provides no grasping, placing, or pushing primitives (Sec. 4A.3), AMP1 builds these skills itself, anew in each episode (Fig. 3E). (These statistics are reported for AMP1 paired with Opus 5.5.) The most frequent skills are routine geometric habits: AMP1 measures a container before placing into it in 66% of episodes, aligns its grasp with the object’s axes in 61%, and reasons about an object’s long and short axes in 47%. When the harness rejects a proposed motion, AMP1 reads the reason and repairs the plan (40% of episodes). When a motion fails during execution, it diagnoses the cause before replanning (39%).

Together, these observations suggest that AMP1 can synthesize manipulation skills from the perception and control interfaces it is given, adapting its strategies to object geometry, execution failures, and contact constraints. Since these behaviors were neither specified in the prompt nor supplied as predefined skills, they provide qualitative evidence that code generation enables the agent to translate its reasoning into task-specific manipulation procedures. Many such skills recur across RoboLab-120 episodes (Tab. S2).

2C Learning from Experience

Thus far, the agent has been evaluated zero-shot, starting every episode from scratch with no memory of its past experience. In the field, however, a robot may be able to build on its experience. We therefore investigate whether the agent can improve with experience, both within a task via few-shot learning and across tasks via continual learning. In the few-shot setting, the agent practices on the same task with resets. In the continual setting, it learns across different tasks as it tackles them in sequence.

We evaluate learning from experience on RoboDojo [25], a challenging benchmark that comprises 42 simulated bimanual manipulation tasks across five capability dimensions (Sec. 4E). RoboDojo provides many layouts per task, so a given task can be practiced on certain scenes and tested on others. Unlike in RoboLab-120, the agent receives only RGB images, without depth or camera calibration. While AMP1 approaches saturation on RoboLab-120 zero-shot (Sec. 2A.1), RoboDojo leaves ample headroom for learning from experience.

In both the few-shot and the continual settings, the agent keeps whatever it finds useful in a persistent memory ℳ\mathcal{M}, a folder that it reads at the start of every episode. We impose no format on ℳ\mathcal{M}, so it may hold notes, code, or data in any form. Typically, the agent decides to keep a Markdown file of notes (strategies that succeeded or failed, pitfalls and observations, useful constants and parameters) and a Python library of code it found useful. Later episodes can read the notes and import and call the Python code. We refer to the harness augmented by the persistent memory ℳ\mathcal{M} as AMP1+.

In the few-shot setting, we let the agent learn a task by practicing it on several layouts until the agent judges that it can reliably succeed or reaches its practice budget. Each practice episode presents a new layout. The only feedback the agent receives is the benchmark’s official binary reward for each episode. This requires no expert demonstrations, no additional model training, and no reward shaping.

In the continual setting, we test whether the agent can accumulate useful knowledge over its lifetime, applying lessons from earlier tasks to later ones. In this setting, the agent tackles an episode of each of the 42 RoboDojo tasks in random order. A persistent memory store ℳ\mathcal{M} is carried across tasks and the agent is instructed to keep only general lessons that may help with any task in the given robot embodiment.

Our approach to learning from experience is gradient-free: the agent revises its memory and code, while the model weights remain fixed. This differs structurally from gradient-based approaches to few-shot learning [45] and continual learning [46, 47], which adapt neural network weights to new experience. Learning without weight updates has precedents in agents that retain verbal reflections [48, 49] or accumulate executable skills [50]. In robotics, ASPIRE retains validated repair knowledge [36], RoboSkill consolidates execution records into reusable guidance and code [51], and RAX builds autonomous control programs and a persistent skill library through exploration [29]. ENPIRE automates policy improvement on physical robots, including both program refinement and gradient-based policy training [52]. We study gradient-free few-shot and continual learning with the generalist model continuing to reason and command the manipulator during execution, measuring both improvement on practiced tasks and transfer and retention across tasks.

Few-shot learning.

AMP1+ practices each task over several rounds. To save wall-clock time, each round runs a batch of BB episodes in parallel. We build the memory ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} iteratively over rounds k=0,1,…{k=0,1,\ldots}, starting from an empty memory store ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} (zero-shot). At round kk, BB instances of AMP1+, each with memory bank ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k}, run on different practice layouts, and the benchmark scores each episode with a binary reward rk,b∈{0,1}r_{k,b}\in\{0,1\}, b=1,…,Bb=1,\dots,B. We denote by τk,b\tau_{k,b} the episode’s transcript, the turn-by-turn record of its messages, code, outputs, and camera images. When the round ends, one of the BB AMP1+ instances from the batch continues after its episode to reflect on the round, with its own episode still in context. It sees all rewards and transcripts so far (rj,br_{j,b} and τj,b\tau_{j,b} for 0≤j≤k0\leq j\leq k and 1≤b≤B1\leq b\leq B), and hence the success rate of each round, as well as the memories ℳ0,…,ℳk\mathcal{M}_{0},\dots,\mathcal{M}_{k}. It then populates ℳk+1\mathcal{M}_{k+1} and decides whether to stop practicing. Practice ends when the reflecting agent decides to stop or after N/BN/B rounds, for a budget of NN practice episodes. In our experiments, we use B=4B=4 and N=48N=48, so practice takes place over up to 12 rounds. The memory bank produced by the ultimate practice round is then frozen as ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} and used for evaluation. AMP1+ itself, in practice and at evaluation, sees only its memory, ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} or ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star}. The rewards and transcripts are available only to the reflecting agent.

Practice raises AMP1+’s success rate on RoboDojo from 26.4% zero-shot to 84.1%, above every entry on the RoboDojo leaderboard. The strongest leaderboard entry at the time of writing, Q0-Preview, reaches 68.9%. Fig. 4F and G show how success rates and efficiency change over the rounds of practice. We measure efficiency by the number of model calls per episode. Each call is one request from the harness to the generalist model to provide its next response. The harness then executes any tool calls specified in that response, such as running code that reads camera images, queries the robot’s pose, computes trajectories, or moves the robot. Efficiency improves almost entirely in the first rounds. By k=2k=2, the memories of 39 of the 42 tasks hold a code library, and later episodes call it instead of rediscovering the procedure, which halves the number of model calls. Later rounds fix remaining failures and continue to raise the success rate without further reducing the number of model calls per episode. Practice ends early for 26 of the 42 tasks, and the other 16 use the full budget of practice rounds.

Fig. 4B–E walk through one example, a task drawn from Mahjong. The agent is asked to take a tile from the stack and stand it upright at the right-hand end of its row; it is not told that the tile must also be the right way up, which the task’s scoring requires. At k=2k=2, one practice episode fails and another succeeds. In its reflection, the agent enlarges the last camera frame of each and sees that the tile’s red symbol is at the bottom in the successful episode, like its neighbors’, but on top in the unsuccessful episode. Tracing both episodes’ actions, it finds that they picked up the face-down tile from opposite ends, and records which end is the tile’s top. After one more round, in which the agent learns to open the gripper before reaching for the tile on the stack, every practice episode succeeds, and success on held-out layouts rises from 10% prior to practice to 100%.

Continual learning.

Starting from an empty initialization ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}, AMP1+ attempts the tt-th task (t=1,…​42t=1,\ldots 42) with memory bank ℳt−1\mathcal{M}_{t-1}, is told whether it succeeded, and produces an updated memory bank ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t}. After one pass through a random permutation of the 42 tasks, the agent’s success rate on all tasks rises from 26.4% zero-shot to 57.6% with ℳ42\mathcal{M}_{42}. To track the gain over the sequence, both on tasks that have already been seen and on tasks that have not yet been seen, we split the task sequence into four segments: S1S_{1} (tasks 1–10), S2S_{2} (11–20), S3S_{3} (21–30), and S4S_{4} (31–42). At the end of segment ii, we evaluate AMP1+ with the memory bank ℳ10​i\mathcal{M}_{10i} on all 42 tasks. Most of the gain in the success rate arrives with the first segment. Experience helps with efficiency as well (Fig. 4I, J).

Figure 4K breaks this gain down segment by segment. Segments that have not yet been seen benefit along with segments that the agent already worked through. This implies that much of what the agent learns from earlier tasks transfers to new tasks. For example, success rate on S4S_{4} rises from 24% without memory to 47% after performing S1S_{1} alone. Segments seen earlier (blue) stay well above their no-memory success rates, so learning on later segments does not erase earlier gains.

What AMP1+ writes into its memory explains these results. From the earliest episodes, it records embodiment-specific knowledge, such as the robot’s coordinate frames, its physical limits, and how to work around the lack of depth sensing and camera calibration. It also writes code for basic manipulation primitives, such as grasping and placing. Because these findings apply to every task, they benefit later episodes as well.

2D Analysis

AMP1 comprises two interlocking parts: the frontier model and the harness. The latter serves as the former’s interface to the world, supplying the sensory inputs and executing the commanded actions. We separate the contributions of these two parts via controlled experiments on RoboLab-120, varying the sensory input and motion interface on the harness side, and the choice of model and its reasoning effort on the model side (Fig. 5). We report a number of findings. First, the model matters far more than any change to the harness (Sec. 2D.1). Second, stronger models do better when they command the manipulator directly rather than via a motion interface that adds assistive routines for grasping and placing objects (Sec. 2D.2). Third, stronger models cope better with missing sensory input and can compensate for impaired sensor constellations via active perception and additional computation (Sec. 2D.3). Fourth, direct image input is substantially more effective than textual descriptions (Sec. 2D.3), contrasting with findings reported in prior work [18].

2D.1 The choice of model dominates performance

We hold the harness fixed and vary the model and its reasoning effort (Fig. 5A). We test 13 models: seven closed models, namely Gemini 4 Argon and six Claude models (Opus 5.5, Opus 5, Opus 4.5, Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Haiku 5.5), and six open-weight models, namely three Qwen models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next), GLM-5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and Kimi K3. Each runs at a low and a high reasoning setting, except Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, which we run with reasoning off and at maximum, and Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, which we run at low and maximum.

The choice of model has the largest effect.

Success rates range from 12.8% with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B to 85.6% with Gemini 4 Argon. Stronger models consistently outperform weaker or older ones: within the Claude family, the success rate is 82.8% with Opus 5.5, 51.6% with the smaller Haiku 5.5, and 35.2% with the older Opus 4.5. Among open-weight models, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves the highest success rate, 64.9%.

Reasoning helps all models.

Claude models gain the most from reasoning, up to 17.2 points for Sonnet 5.5 and 14.6 points for Opus 5.5. Gemini 4 Argon gains only 2.3 points, partly because it has little headroom: it already succeeds in most episodes at low reasoning, and more than half of its remaining failures are in tasks where reasoning is not the limiting factor (Supplementary Materials, Sec. S6).

2D.2 Assistive routines help weaker models but hinder stronger ones

We compare two motion interfaces for every model on RoboLab-120, each at its more-reasoning setting (Fig. 5B): the basic harness, our default, in which AMP1 commands timed end-effector waypoints directly, and an assistive harness, which adds routines that plan and execute picks and placements for the agent. Both use the same prompt and perception.

Basic harness.

AMP1 commands motion as a trajectory of timed end-effector poses and gripper commands, and makes all decisions, from where to grasp an object to where to release it. The agent can preview a trajectory before executing it. The harness refuses motions that are unreachable or too fast, but leaves collision checking to the model (Sec. 4A.3).

Assistive harness.

The assistive harness lets the model delegate grasping and placing through additional routines. The model can request ranked grasp and placement poses. A motion planner executes collision-free picks and placements at the indicated poses. The assistive pick routines check whether the object is held and retry with another grasp if not (Sec. 4A.3). The model still decides which objects to move, in what order, and when the task is complete. It can always take full control via the basic harness, which remains available at all times.

Result.

The four models with the highest success rates under the basic harness – Gemini 4 Argon, Opus 5.5, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5.5 – all do worse with the assistive harness, by up to 7.5 points (Fig. 5B). The six models with the lowest success rates all do better, by up to 17.6 points for the weakest model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The three models in between gain nothing.

Analysis.

Prior work found that high-level abstractions improved single-turn performance, while multi-turn reasoning could compensate for lower-level interfaces [18]. Our results indicate that assistive grasping and placing routines help weaker models but reduce the success rate of stronger models. The assistive routines are imperfect: a grasp can slip or a placement can miss. Weaker models still benefit from the assistance, because the routines succeed more often than their own direct grasping and placement attempts. For stronger models, the assistive routines are on balance a detrimental distraction, because they hide failures that the models could otherwise immediately observe and correct. For example, an assistive pick routine retries internally before the model can intervene, and reports only whether it succeeded, not what went wrong. With the basic harness, the model sees the result of every atomic action and can correct mistakes as they happen.

2D.3 The effects of sensory impairment

RoboLab-120 provides fixed scene cameras and a wrist camera, each with RGB images, depth (D), and calibration (C). On top of these signals, the AMP1 harness offers perception tools (T) that build a scene model from the fused point cloud: they segment it into objects, track the objects over the episode, and render them from any viewpoint (Sec. 4A.2). We ablate this input along two axes. The first is how much geometric information each camera provides: starting from the full input (RGB+C+D+T), we remove perception tools (RGB+C+D), then depth (RGB+C), and then calibration (RGB). The second is which cameras AMP1 sees through: all of them, the scene cameras only, or the wrist camera only. In a final condition (Text), AMP1 receives no images, only textual descriptions of their content, as recommended in prior work [18]. The rest of the harness and the prompt are unchanged.

Stronger models rebuild missing geometry at the cost of efficiency.

With a strong model (Opus 5.5) and all cameras, removing geometric information lowers the success rate only modestly but carries a cost in terms of efficiency (Fig. 5C). From RGB+C+D+T to RGB+C+D, RGB+C, and RGB, the success rate declines from 82.8% to 81.9%, 81.1%, and 75.8%, while the mean number of model calls per episode rises from 34.8 to 38.7, 46.3, and 53.5, respectively. AMP1 rebuilds the missing geometry itself. Without the perception tools, it detects objects in the images and lifts them to 3D with depth and calibration. Without depth, it picks matching pixels in zoomed crops of different views and triangulates them through the known calibration. Without calibration, it first estimates the camera parameters, most reliably with the wrist camera, which it can move (a form of active perception [53]): it captures images at known gripper poses, matches SIFT features across them [54], and fits the focal length, principal point, and camera-to-gripper pose by least squares (Supplementary Materials, Sec. S4.1).

Weaker models require a more robust sensor constellation.

Fig. 5C compares Opus 5.5 with three weaker models: Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Opus 4.5. While Opus 5.5 is able to compensate for missing sensory input at the cost of efficiency, weaker models are more brittle. The weaker the model, the more sensitive it is to sensory impairment. The success rate of Opus 4.5 drops sharply as soon as the perception tools are taken away. Haiku 5.5 suffers when the perception tools and depth are both withheld. Sonnet 5.5 exhibits material degradation in task completion when the perception tools, depth, and calibration are all removed. The gap between the stronger and weaker models is particularly stark when only RGB input is provided; in this condition, Haiku 5.5 succeeds in only 10.7% of the episodes, against 75.8% for Opus 5.5. Weaker models are unable to compensate for sensory impairment even with more reasoning and computation: as sensory input is ablated, AMP1 with Opus 5.5 takes substantially more model calls to complete the tasks, while with weaker models the number of model calls does not grow by much as their success rate plummets.

Images cannot be replaced by text.

Prior work recommended substituting direct camera feeds by textual descriptions of their contents [18]. We test this with four Claude models: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Opus 4.5. In the Text condition, a second instance of the same model describes what the cameras see. AMP1 receives these descriptions in place of images. The results are summarized in Fig. 5C. With Opus 5.5, the success rate drops from 75.8% with RGB images to 36.8% with the corresponding textual descriptions. The success rate of weaker models in the Text condition is vanishingly low. Textual descriptions elide geometric detail, such as whether the gripper is aligned with an object; this has a sharply detrimental effect on task performance.

Multiple cameras are not necessary.

With a strong model (Opus 5.5), AMP1 is robust to removing all but one camera from the sensor constellation (Fig. 5D). Specifically, in the RGB+C+D+T condition, the agent has an 82.8% success rate with all cameras, 80.8% with the scene cameras only, and 80.0% with the wrist camera only. The spread is confined to three percentage points in all image-based conditions. With only the wrist camera, AMP1 compensates by means of active perception [53]: it first pulls the arm back to bring more of the scene into view.

3 Discussion

3A AMP1 versus other manipulation policies

The policies we compare against fall into four classes: learned policies, skill orchestration, offline program synthesis, and agentic manipulation policies (AMPs). Learned policies, including VLAs and WAMs, map observations to actions end-to-end from robot data. Skill orchestration policies can utilize generalist AI models to sequence pre-existing low-level skills; their performance is thus limited by the reliability of those skills. In offline program synthesis, a generalist AI model writes or refines a control program before deployment; the program can incorporate perception and feedback, but the model does not revise the control strategy as the task unfolds. AMPs keep the generalist model in the control loop, where it can interpret new observations and directly command the manipulator.

Learned policies.

At the time of writing, the strongest learned policies on the RoboLab-120 leaderboard – Lakeside, BiMind v0.5, and FLUX 3 Action – succeed in 51.0%, 49.2%, and 42.9% of episodes, respectively, in contrast to 85.6% for AMP1 when paired with Gemini 4 Argon and 82.8% when paired with Opus 5.5. AMP1 perceives the environment with the aid of RGB, depth, and camera calibration, whereas typical VLAs and WAMs use RGB alone. The richer sensory input, however, does not explain the gap: when paired with Opus 5.5, AMP1 still succeeds in 81.1% of episodes without depth, and in 75.8% with RGB input alone (Fig. 5C). AMP1 draws on the broad intelligence of the generalist AI model to decide which objects to move, in what order, and how to react to unanticipated challenges (Sec. 2B), whereas a learned policy must acquire its skills from robot data. In addition to their overall poor task performance, specialist manipulation policies are particularly brittle to changes in the phrasing of the task: in the ‘vague’ task specification condition on RoboLab-120, the success rate of FLUX 3 Action drops further to 28.4%, while AMP1 remains at 84.0% and 79.8% with Gemini 4 Argon and Opus 5.5, respectively.

Skill orchestration.

Harness VLA [37] and HarnessPAI [12] delegate motion to a learned VLA policy, so their reliability is bounded by that learned policy. Like the routines of our assistive harness, but to an even greater degree, a VLA is something of a black box: when it fails, the agent has limited ability to understand the causes and potential mitigations (Sec. 2D.2). HarnessPAI compensates for this limitation through practice, refining its program over several trial runs of the evaluation tasks. AMP1 reaches comparable results zero-shot: 95.2% against 96.5% on LIBERO-PRO, and 100.0% against 96.3% on robosuite (Sec. 2A.1).

Offline program synthesis.

On LIBERO-PRO and robosuite, ASPIRE [36] refines a program for each task through repeated execution and debugging, then evaluates the resulting program on held-out configurations. The program can use perception and feedback, but the generalist model does not revise it during deployment. AMP1 is evaluated zero-shot on these benchmarks, with the generalist model in the control loop.

Agentic manipulation policies.

CaP-Agent0 [18] also keeps a coding model in the control loop. Its harness supplies a learned grasp planner and a library of synthesized geometric utilities, and uses a separate vision-language model to create a textual summary of changes in the scene. The authors found that this textual representation improved performance relative to direct image input. In our experiments, replacing images with textual descriptions is detrimental to task performance. Adding assistive grasping and placing routines also reduces the success rate of stronger models (Sec. 2D).

Astranomy is a concurrent AMP that is based on GPT-6 Astra and was evaluated in simulation on the RoboLab-120 benchmark [21]. Astranomy reaches 74.8% on RoboLab-120, in comparison to 85.6% for AMP1 with Gemini 4 Argon. Beyond the underlying model, the harnesses differ in three ways. First, Astranomy queries the model for one small end-effector step at a time, whereas AMP1 commands a trajectory. Second, Astranomy disables code execution, whereas AMP1 acts by means of code. Third, the AMP1 harness equips the agent with an editable scene model. Equalizing the underlying model makes the effect of the harness even more salient: Astranomy reports a 25.3% success rate on a 30-task subset with Opus 5.5, in comparison to AMP1’s 84.7% with the same model on the same subset of tasks.

3B Outlook

AMP1 has a number of limitations. First, the policy is slow as the robot spends much of each episode waiting for the model to reason. Second, the model cannot reconsider a trajectory while it executes: our evaluations largely concern quasi-static scenes, whereas a moving target or a slipping object may require a response before the model’s next turn.

Notwithstanding these limitations, our results indicate that AMPs constitute a promising foundation for robot manipulation. They cannot yet be deployed in mission-critical settings, but neither can the alternatives. Specialist manipulation policies, such as VLAs and WAMs, are comparably fast but unreliable. AMPs are comparably reliable but slow. We see a promising path to practical manipulation in using AMPs as a starting point for developing manipulation systems that are both reliable and fast. A general trend that supports this optimism is that the cost of a given capability level has fallen by roughly an order of magnitude per year [26, 27]. Thus we can expect the cost of a model call (the ‘thinking’ part of an AMP’s execution) to asymptote to zero over time.

Beyond these general trends, the harness itself offers several avenues for acceleration. Our few-shot and continual learning experiments show that the agent can retain useful code and reduce the number of model calls across episodes (Sec. 2C). Reusing these routines avoids repeatedly writing code for calibration, geometric computations, and basic motions. Fast local feedback controllers could be synthesized from AMP experience [29]. AMP execution traces could also provide supervision for learned policies [11, 31]. And the model could plan the next motion while the current one executes, thus overlapping thinking with acting.

4 Materials and Methods

4A Harness

At the core of AMP1 is a harness through which a generalist AI model perceives, acts, and reflects (Fig. 6). The harness comprises (a) an SDK that is called by the model from a persistent Python interpreter (Sec. 4B); (b) a robot server that serves the SDK’s requests: it returns camera images, depth and the robot’s state, segments the point cloud into objects and tracks them over the episode, and checks and executes the robot’s motion; (c) a route policy that sets which of these requests the harness allows; and (d) reference documentation for the SDK, which is appended to the model’s system prompt. Parts (b) and (c) are omitted from Fig. 6 for clarity.

In zero-shot evaluation, everything the model knows about the task and the robot comes through the harness: the instruction, the camera images, depth and calibration, the robot’s proprioception, the segmented objects, and the remaining control steps and time. The instruction is read by the model through the SDK in its first turn, together with its first view of the scene.

The harness defines two frames for each end-effector. The end-effector (EE) frame is positioned at the base of the gripper. The tool center point (TCP) frame lies at a fixed offset from the EE frame: its origin, the TCP, is centered between the finger pads, and its axes point along the gripper’s approach and closing directions. The model commands motion and defines all grasp geometry at the TCP.

We describe the SDK’s functions in three groups: sensing, perception, and motion. Motion comes in two harness variants: the basic harness, our default, in which the model itself commands timed TCP waypoints with gripper commands, and the assistive harness, which adds grasping and placing routines to the basic functions.

4A.1 Sensing

AMP1 observes the scene and the robot only through SDK calls in the code it implements, and thus the model decides what to observe and when. The only information added to every result the model receives from executing its code are the remaining control steps and wall-clock time. The model may observe the scene arbitrarily often and it may also execute a motion without prior observation and verify its outcome afterwards from the robot’s state and camera images.

The model reads the instruction, the maximum number of control steps in an episode, and the steps that remain. Since the episode terminates when its horizon is reached, the model can plan its motion against it. It can also read the robot specification such as its cameras, its workspace, the joint limits and the default configuration, and, for each end effector, its gripper geometry and TCP frame.

The robot’s state comprises the measured joint positions q~∈ℝn\tilde{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and the poses of the EE and TCP frames in the robot’s base frame; we denote the measured TCP pose by T~∈S​E​(3)\tilde{T}\in SE(3). It also includes the gripper state g~∈[0,1]\tilde{g}\in[0,1] (0 open, 1 closed) and the last gripper command g∈{0,1}g\in\{0,1\}.

For each camera, the model can read its RGB image, a depth image subsampled from the RGB image’s resolution by a fixed stride, the intrinsics KK, and the camera’s current pose Tbase,cam∈S​E​(3)T_{\mathrm{base,cam}}\in SE(3) in the robot’s base frame. Helper functions convert between the image and 3D coordinates. One projects a 3D point into the image through Tbase,cam−1T_{\mathrm{base,cam}}^{-1} and KK, returning its pixel coordinates and its depth along the optical axis, and another inverts this projection for a given pixel and depth. The model can also request a colored point cloud combined from all cameras.

With the rendering functions provided by the harness, the model can compose its own views of the scene from these inputs and the perceived objects. It can draw 3D elements, such as points, boxes, object identifiers, target poses or a planned motion, onto a real camera image by projecting them through Tbase,cam−1T_{\mathrm{base,cam}}^{-1} and KK, for example to check whether a planned grasp is aligned with the object. It can also render a point cloud, perceived objects, and the robot from any virtual viewpoint, and request a close-up of an object that combines renders from viewpoints around the object. All of these views are built from the robot’s own sensor data and the perceived scene model (Sec. 4A.2).

An image enters the model’s context only when the model chooses to look at it; that is, when its code displays the image. Every displayed image is also saved. Once the context exceeds a fixed number or total size of images, the oldest are replaced by pointers to their saved files, and the model can reload any of them with a dedicated tool. The model can also keep information from earlier turns, such as images and depth maps, in its persistent interpreter, for example to compare a scene before and after a motion.

4A.2 Perception

The harness maintains a scene model, a set of objects ojo_{j}, each occupying a region Mj⊂ℝ3M_{j}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}. It segments a fused point cloud into voxel clusters and extrudes the height map of each cluster into a closed mesh that bounds MjM_{j}. The union of these regions forms the obstacle region 𝒪=⋃jMj\mathcal{O}=\bigcup_{j}M_{j} against which collisions are checked. The generalist AI model can exclude objects (such as the one it is about to grasp) from a collision check. A stereo matching model can be used to estimate depth from stereo images (Sec. 4F).

At each update of the scene model, the harness voxelizes the fused point cloud and clusters the voxels into candidate objects as connected components of adjacent voxels. The clustering stops where one object touches another and at sharp color discontinuities. Small fragments, such as an isolated face, are merged into a larger nearby segment of similar color, and close segments of the same color are joined. Segments that remain very small are dropped as noise. Each object is then represented as a closed mesh by extruding its top surface downwards to its lowest observed point. Occluded gaps in the top surface are filled unless the cameras have seen them. Geometry is therefore inferred from depth, while color serves as a secondary criterion that separates touching objects.

The scene model is updated in the background whenever a new camera frame is available and no motion is running, before every collision check, and whenever the generalist AI model requests it. Each object ojo_{j} has a unique identifier, a label naming its color and dimensions, its centroid, axis aligned and oriented bounding boxes, and the mesh bounding MjM_{j}. The generalist AI model can list objects, read their points, size and color, filter them by label, color or size, and sort them by distance to a 3D point.

Each update matches its objects to those in the previous update by a minimal cost assignment, which pairs two objects only if their centroids lie within a distance dmd_{\mathrm{m}} and their colors and sizes agree within tolerances; a matched object keeps its identifier. When an object is merged with another, split, or keeps its place but no longer matches because its appearance changed, its old identifier resolves to the object that now covers most of its footprint, while an object that moved farther than dmd_{\mathrm{m}} receives a new identifier. An object that is not seen in an observation update, for example, because the arm occludes it, leaves the scene model, but its identifier is reserved for a fixed time. An object of similar color and size that reappears within dmd_{\mathrm{m}} of where it was last seen receives the old identifier. Each update also reports what it removed and changed, so that the generalist AI model can follow how the scene model evolves.

The generalist AI model can also correct the scene model. It can grow an object from a single pixel through neighboring points. It can define an object from an axis-aligned or oriented box or from a set of points. And it can replace and remove wrong or spurious objects. Objects that are added by the generalist AI model persist across perception updates and take precedence over the perceived objects they overlap. The system prompt warns the generalist AI model that perception can merge touching objects, split one object in two, or fill in hidden parts incorrectly. It instructs the generalist AI model to check the perceived objects against the camera images and, when they are incorrect, to repair the scene model with these tools rather than compensate for the error in its plans. After every motion, the generalist AI model is instructed to update the scene model and look at the cameras.

4A.3 Motion

The generalist AI model writes code that produces a trajectory of TCP poses with gripper commands, given as timed waypoints wi=(Ti,ti,gi){w_{i}=(T_{i},t_{i},g_{i})}, i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N. Each waypoint consists of (a) a desired TCP pose Ti=(pi,Ri)∈S​E​(3)T_{i}=(p_{i},R_{i})\in SE(3) in the robot’s base frame, with position pi∈ℝ3p_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and orientation Ri∈S​O​(3)R_{i}\in SO(3), (b) the desired arrival time tit_{i}, and (c) a gripper command gi∈{0,1}g_{i}\in\{0,1\} (open or closed). The model typically constructs each waypoint’s TCP pose relative to a reference it has measured, such as the current TCP pose, an object’s centroid, or the pose of another waypoint, using helper functions that either build a pose from a position and an approach direction (for example, top-down at a given yaw) or shift a pose along its own axes. The harness provides no function that chooses grasps or placements; those decisions are left to the generalist model. For a bimanual robot, the model generates a sequence of waypoints for each arm.

From the waypoints, the harness computes a joint space trajectory τ:[0,tN]→𝒞\tau\colon[0,t_{N}]\to\mathcal{C}, where 𝒞⊂ℝn\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is the configuration space of the robot’s nn joints, with configurations q∈𝒞q\in\mathcal{C}. Starting from the current TCP pose T0=(p0,R0)=f⁡(q0)T_{0}=(p_{0},R_{0})=f(q_{0}) at t0=0t_{0}=0, where f:𝒞→S​E​(3)f\colon\mathcal{C}\to SE(3) is the forward kinematics, the harness interpolates between consecutive waypoints, treating position and orientation separately rather than as a single screw motion (the decoupled path of Sec. 9.2.1 in [55]). More precisely, for tt in the segment [ti−1,ti][t_{i-1},t_{i}] between waypoints i−1i-1 and ii, the interpolated TCP pose is T⁡(t)=(p⁡(t),R⁡(t))T(t)=(p(t),R(t)) with p⁡(t)=pi−1+σ⁡(u)​(pi−pi−1){p(t)=p_{i-1}+\sigma(u)\,(p_{i}-p_{i-1})} and R⁡(t)=Ri−1​exp⁡(σ⁡(u)​log⁡(Ri−1⊤​Ri)){R(t)=R_{i-1}\exp\!\big(\sigma(u)\log(R_{i-1}^{\top}R_{i})\big)}. Here, pip_{i} and RiR_{i} are the position and orientation of the waypoint ii, u=(t−ti−1)/(ti−ti−1)∈[0,1]{u=(t-t_{i-1})/(t_{i}-t_{i-1})\in[0,1]} is the normalized time within the segment, and σ\sigma is a quintic polynomial time scaling that minimizes jerk.

At every control step kk of duration Δ​t\Delta t, the harness computes qk=τ⁡(k​Δ​t){q_{k}=\tau(k\,\Delta t)} by damped least squares inverse kinematics of T⁡(k​Δ​t)=(p⁡(k​Δ​t),R⁡(k​Δ​t)){T(k\,\Delta t)=(p(k\,\Delta t),R(k\,\Delta t))}, seeded with qk−1q_{k-1}. The numerical inverse kinematics solver always returns the best configuration qkq_{k} it can find for an interpolated pose T⁡(k​Δ​t)T(k\,\Delta t), but when the pose is unreachable or the solver does not converge, qkq_{k} reaches it only approximately. The harness therefore validates the trajectory and executes it only if the following conditions hold at every step kk. First, the position and orientation errors between f⁡(qk)f(q_{k}) and T⁡(k​Δ​t)T(k\,\Delta t) must lie within specified tolerances. Second, each joint’s speed must stay below its speed limit. Approaching near the end of a joint’s range of motion or near a singularity only sends a warning to the model. Additionally, the model can also test whether τ\tau lies in 𝒞free=𝒞∖𝒞obs\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}}=\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{obs}}, where 𝒞obs={q∈𝒞∣𝒜⁡(q)∩𝒪≠∅}\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\{q\in\mathcal{C}\mid\mathcal{A}(q)\cap\mathcal{O}\neq\emptyset\}, by checking configurations it samples from τ\tau. Here, 𝒜⁡(q)⊂ℝ3\mathcal{A}(q)\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} is the region occupied by the robot at configuration qq, which the harness approximates by spheres covering the arm and the gripper, and 𝒪\mathcal{O} is the obstacle region formed by the perceived objects (Sec. 4A.2). A refused trajectory is returned with the reason and the affected steps, so that the model can repair it. Before planning a motion, the model can also test whether a single pose is reachable, with the same tolerances.

Once the entire trajectory has passed these checks, the harness executes it by sending the robot the computed absolute joint position targets, one qkq_{k} per control step, each with the current gripper command.

4B Python Interpreter

The agent acts primarily through a Python interpreter, which executes the code implemented by the model in a kernel that persists during the entire episode. The kernel keeps imports, variables, and the functions the model defines between calls, so that the information it generates in one turn can be reused in later ones. Each call returns the code’s printed output, any error with its traceback, and the images the code displays, followed by the remaining control steps and wall-clock time. The model reads the result at the start of its next turn. The model has a number of auxiliary tools in addition to the interpreter, such as reloading an image saved earlier, and ending the episode.

In the basic harness, the motion interface only previews, checks, and executes waypoints and gripper commands. Everything in between – from choosing a grasp to measuring a container, pushing an object, or recovering from a refused trajectory – the model implements itself, combining SDK calls with its own geometry code. In zero-shot evaluation, each episode starts from a new sandboxed kernel, so the model writes its skills from scratch every time. Section S3 in the Supplementary Materials shows how the model builds such skills during one episode, turn by turn. When learning from experience, the model can decide to save its skills into the memory store ℳ\mathcal{M} (Sec. 2C).

4C RoboLab

RoboLab-120 comprises 120 language-specified pick-and-place tasks simulated in Isaac Sim [22]. Each task is posed with three variants of its instruction: default, vague, and specific.

Embodiment setup.

The robot is a simulated Franka Panda arm in the DROID configuration, with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, mounted at a table. Physics runs at 120 Hz and control at 15 Hz. Each action specifies seven absolute joint positions and a gripper command. Two fixed over-the-shoulder cameras and a wrist camera render 1280×7201280\times 720 images, with horizontal fields of view of about 104∘104^{\circ} and 88∘88^{\circ}, respectively.

Evaluation protocol.

Following the benchmark’s published protocol, we run 10 episodes per task (i.e., 1,200 in total) for each of the three instruction variants. All episodes of a task start from the same initial scene, so they differ only through the policy and simulator nondeterminism. An episode succeeds at the first step at which the task’s success condition holds, and fails if the task’s time limit, between 20 and 300 s of simulated time, expires first. The simulation is paused while the agent reasons, perceives, and plans, so only executed motion counts against this limit. The agent receives the robot model (kinematics, joint limits, and collision geometry). Depth is rendered without noise, and camera intrinsics and extrinsics are exact.

4D CaP-Gym

CaP-Gym [18] wraps three simulation benchmarks behind a common interface: LIBERO-PRO [32], robosuite [33], and BEHAVIOR-1K [34]. Following the published protocol, we evaluate three of the four LIBERO-PRO suites (LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-Spatial), all seven robosuite tasks, and two BEHAVIOR-1K tasks.

Embodiment setup.

The embodiment differs across benchmarks. LIBERO-PRO and robosuite simulate a Franka Panda arm with its standard parallel-jaw gripper in MuJoCo [56]. Physics runs at 500 Hz and control at 20 Hz. Each action specifies seven absolute joint positions and a gripper command. In robosuite, the two bimanual tasks use two opposing Panda arms. (The ‘spill wipe’ task replaces the gripper with a wiping tool.) BEHAVIOR-1K simulates a Galaxea R1Pro mobile manipulator in OmniGibson on Isaac Sim, with a holonomic base, a four-joint torso, and two seven-joint arms with parallel-jaw grippers, controlled at 30 Hz. LIBERO-PRO uses a fixed camera and a wrist camera at 800×512800\times 512. robosuite uses a single camera at 512×512512\times 512. BEHAVIOR-1K uses a head camera and two wrist cameras at 512×512512\times 512.

Evaluation protocol.

We follow CaP-Gym’s environment protocol, including its tasks, controllers, cameras, step horizon, and success checks. LIBERO-PRO perturbs each of its 30 tasks in two ways, swapping object positions or changing the instruction to name a different object, yielding 60 tasks with 50 trials each (i.e., 3,000 episodes). Robosuite runs 100 trials per task (i.e., 700 episodes), with object positions randomized at every reset. BEHAVIOR-1K runs 25 trials per task (i.e., 50 episodes), each starting from a fixed, pre-sampled scene instance. Each episode is limited by the environment’s step horizon: 8,000 steps for LIBERO-PRO and 1,000–5,000 for robosuite. BEHAVIOR-1K has no step horizon and is bounded only by wall-clock time. As in RoboLab, the simulation is paused while the agent reasons, so only executed motion counts against the horizon. Depth and camera calibration are part of CaP-Gym’s observations. Depth is rendered without noise, and camera intrinsics and extrinsics are exact.

4E RoboDojo

RoboDojo [25] comprises 42 bimanual manipulation tasks simulated in Isaac Sim, grouped into five categories: generalization (12 tasks), memory (6), long-horizon (8), precision (8), and open-ended (8).

Embodiment setup.

The robot consists of two ARX X5 arms with six joints and a parallel-jaw gripper on each, mounted at fixed bases on a table. Physics runs at 250 Hz and control at 25 Hz. Each action specifies six absolute joint positions and a gripper command per arm. A head camera and two wrist cameras render 640×480640\times 480 images, with horizontal fields of view of about 96∘96^{\circ} and 78∘78^{\circ}, respectively.

Evaluation protocol.

We conduct our few-shot learning and continual learning experiments on RoboDojo (Sec. 2C). The benchmark defines three public evaluation seeds (0, 1, and 2), each specifying 50 predetermined layouts per task with variations in objects, their positions, backgrounds, and clutter. We use seed 0 for experience collection. In few-shot learning, practice is run five times per task, and the run with the highest success rate in seed 1 is selected for each task. In both few-shot and continual learning, we report success rates on seed 2. We calculate the success rate as the public leaderboard does. Each category’s success rate is the mean over its tasks, and the overall success rate is the mean over the five categories. Confidence intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals over tasks, resampled within each category. As in RoboLab, simulation is paused while the agent reasons. We follow the input protocol of the GPT-6 Astra entry on the public leaderboard, submitted by the RoboDojo authors [57]. For camera data, the agent receives only RGB images, without depth or camera calibration. Each task instruction is accompanied by a task recipe that describes the scene and gives a scoring rubric. Four tasks also have task notes, which we summarize here. In ‘imitate sorting sequence’, the robot must hold still through the demonstration and then reproduce the observed order. In ‘make kong’, it must wait for the opponent’s discard and then declare the kong in two motions. In ‘match and pick from conveyor’, the belt does not stop, so the grasp must be aimed where the object will be. In ‘play tic-tac-toe’, the robot must hold still during the opponent’s turns, play to win or block, and place all five pieces.

4F Real-world trials

Harness.

We made minimal adjustments to the harness SDK’s reference documentation, replacing simulation references with their real-world equivalents. To support recovery from errors (RfE), the harness includes two SDK functions: one queries the arm’s state, the other requests robot error recovery. When a Franka collision reflex interrupts motion, the harness reports the error to the model. The model can generate code that calls these functions. The harness executes the code and returns the results. Following successful recovery, the model can command a revised trajectory.

Embodiment setup.

We use the DROID setup [38], comprising a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, a wrist-mounted ZED Mini attached using the official DROID fixture, and two ZED 2i cameras providing left and right shoulder views. The shoulder cameras are positioned to approximate the baseline policies’ training-time camera configuration, with each baseline using its expected views. All cameras operate at 30 fps with an output resolution of 1280×7201280\times 720. When depth is needed, we use a pretrained S2M2 stereo model to obtain metric depth from the ZED cameras [58]. Each methods uses its expected views: π0.5\pi_{0.5} takes the left shoulder and wrist cameras as visual observations [24], whereas FLUX 3 [23] and AMP1 additionally use the right shoulder camera.

Evaluation protocol.

We evaluate each method on 12 complex real-world tasks. To assess robustness to visual and hardware variation, we use three instances of the platform that differ in scene background and hardware characteristics, including camera calibration, cabling, and component wear. For each task and method, we conduct 9 trials, with 3 trials on each platform instance. The instructions are issued in free-form natural language and span single-skill pick-and-place as well as multi-stage instructions that require subgoal sequencing. For fair comparison, we build a scene restoration tool that ensures that, for every trial of each task, the initial object poses (projected into the workspace relative to the robot base) and the set of objects are consistent across all methods. The initial scene and the language instruction for each task are detailed in Supplementary Materials. All methods are evaluated under the same 5-minute execution time budget (excluding reasoning time). If the time limit is exceeded or an uninstructed object is erroneously grasped and placed, the trial is considered unsuccessful. For the baseline deployments and AMP1 without RfE, a robot controller error that interrupts motion also terminates the trial. For AMP1 with RfE, a recoverable controller error does not by itself terminate the trial; the agent can request error recovery through the harness and, if recovery succeeds, continue the same trial within the remaining execution-time budget.

4G Compute

Closed-weight models are queried through their providers’ APIs. Open-weight models are self-hosted with SGLang. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B run on H100 GPUs, the others on B200 GPUs. We do not set sampling parameters such as temperature and top-pp, so each model uses its provider’s defaults. In simulation, multiple episodes run in parallel on a node with eight H100 GPUs, which hosts the simulator together with the harness and the agent’s code execution. On the real robot, the harness runs on a local workstation with two RTX Pro 6000 GPUs. The baseline policies are also evaluated on the same platform.
