5 Supplementary Materials

S1 Real-world trials

This section complements the embodiment setup and the evaluation protocol described in Sec. 4F with more details of our real-world experiments. Fig. S1 shows the three instances of our DROID-based platform. They use the same arm, gripper, and camera models, and differ in tabletop background and in unit-level hardware (camera calibration, cabling, component wear). Every method is run for 3 trials per task on each instance, i.e., 9 trials per task and method. Fig. S2 shows the initial scene and the language instruction of each of the 12 tasks.

In the real-world evaluation results (Tab. 1), the time to success of AMP1 is split into execution (Exec.) and reasoning (Reason.). Execution time covers only the intervals in which the robot is carrying out the agent’s commanded actions; reasoning time accumulates the agent’s inference, the execution of its own code, the camera capture, and the 3D perception processing performed after each motion. In addition, we annotate each of the 12 tasks with three kinds of features, shown in the columns Manip., Horizon, and Reasoning. These features let us relate a method’s success to the demands of a task; we explain each of them in more detail below:

  • •

    Manipulation describes the kinds of actions a task requires. A task is prehensile if it can be solved by grasping and placing objects alone. A task is labeled non-prehensile if completing it requires non-prehensile actions, such as pushing, sliding, or nudging an object, so that purely prehensile manipulation cannot solve it. A task can have both labels when completing it requires both kinds of motion. For example, in the task “Put the bowl on the plate”, the bowl is flipped and no initial grasp is feasible, so the robot first pushes it to the edge of the bin and then grasps it.

  • •

    Horizon separates single-step and multi-step tasks. A single-step task usually involves manipulating only one target object (e.g., picking and placing one object). A multi-step task requires completing multiple subtasks in sequence, usually by manipulating multiple objects one after another (e.g., putting all the red things in the bin).

  • •

    Reasoning lists the kinds of reasoning a task requires to decide what to manipulate and how. Multiple kinds may be called for per task:

    • –

      Spatial reasoning: understanding a spatial relation, e.g., “to the left of”.

    • –

      Semantic grounding: identifying objects from their color or category, e.g., “red things” or “canned foods”.

    • –

      Exclusion: acting on all objects of a class except a named one, e.g., “all the tools except the hammer”.

    • –

      Ordering: deciding the order in which to act, e.g., comparing cup sizes to nest them.

    • –

      Affordance: an enabling action is needed to make the next action feasible, e.g., pushing a flipped bowl to the bin edge before grasping it.

    • –

      Memory: using information that is no longer visible, e.g., remembering which cup hides the yellow cube in order to uncover it.

Complementing the baseline comparison in Tab. 1, we ablate access to the two error-recovery SDK functions in Tab. S1. Without these functions, a robot controller error that interrupts motion terminates the trial under our evaluation protocol. With recovery from error (RfE), the agent can request recovery through the harness and continue the same trial if recovery succeeds. AMP1 succeeds in 104 of 108 trials (96.3%) with RfE and 94 of 108 trials (87.0%) without RfE. The reported average time to success is similar across conditions, although each average includes only the successful trials in that condition. The gain is largest on tasks involving close contact between the gripper or held object and the scene, where collisions are more likely (e.g., “Pack canned foods into the bin”, from 3 / 9 to 9 / 9).

S2 Further illustration of emergent behaviors

Figs. S3 and S4 show the remaining behaviors described in Sec. 2B that did not fit in Fig. 3.

S3 How AMP1 reasons and acts: a turn by turn example

Figure S5 follows one complete episode, on the RoboLab BananaInBowlTask, to demonstrate how AMP1 reasons and acts. The agent runs Claude Opus 5.5 at high reasoning effort with the basic harness. It commands the manipulator by means of timed waypoints with gripper commands. It solves the task in eight turns, in each of which it writes and runs Python code.

The episode exhibits a generic decision loop that repeats across tasks. AMP1 gathers the information needed for the decision, builds its own geometric model of the object to manipulate from the perceived points, previews its motion before executing it, and checks the outcome in images and sensor readings before the next decision.

The first turn starts from a) the system prompt, which describes the robot, the SDK and the rules of the episode, b) the tool definitions, and c) a first user message that withholds the instruction and the remaining steps. AMP1 therefore has no image of the scene yet. Its first implemented code, which follows an example in the system prompt, reads the instruction (“Pick up the banana and place it in the bowl”) and the remaining steps, lists the objects detected by perception, and shows itself two camera views, one annotated with the object identifiers and bounding boxes.

In turn 2, AMP1 builds its own geometric model of the banana. It retrieves the banana’s points, fits an oriented bounding box to them, and reads the end-effector pose and the table height from the robot’s observation. In turn 3, AMP1 plans the grasp. Because the banana is curved, AMP1 reasons that the centroid of its points may not lie on it, so it plans to grasp the banana at the point of the cloud nearest to the centroid, with the fingers closing across the banana’s width, perpendicular to its long axis. It plans timed waypoints for the approach and previews the motion without executing it. The harness confirms that the motion is feasible, and AMP1 then runs a collision check on poses sampled along the previewed path, which reports contacts of the gripper with both the banana and the table. In turn 4, AMP1 accepts the contact with the banana as expected for a grasp, raises the grasp pose slightly so that the fingertips reach approximately the middle of the banana’s height rather than the table, and only then executes the approach. In turn 5, AMP1 checks the wrist camera and finds that the banana sits between the open fingers. It closes the gripper and lifts the banana. In turn 6, AMP1 interprets its gripper reading, which rose from 0.28 after closing to 0.55 after the lift, as the banana slipping or rotating in the grasp. Rather than reusing the bowl position from the first turn, it perceives the scene again to locate the bowl’s center. It then plans to carry the banana high enough to clear the bowl’s rim, and to lower it before opening the gripper. In turn 7, allowing for the banana having rotated in the grasp, it estimates that the banana now hangs about 7 cm below the gripper, so its bottom clears the rim during the carry. It then carries it over the bowl and lowers it. In turn 8, it opens the gripper and plans to raise the empty gripper to look at the result. Finally, RoboLab’s success check detects that the banana has dropped into the bowl and ends the episode.

S4 Case studies

This section walks through a number of episodes in detail, to show how AMP1 reasons, acts, and verifies its progress over the course of a task.

S4.1 Self-calibration of the wrist camera

This case study follows one episode of the RGB-only ablation (Sec. 2D.3, Fig. 5C) on the RoboLab task FoodPacking2CansTask (“Pack canned foods into the bin”). In this setting, AMP1 has access to RGB frames from the two scene cameras and the wrist camera, the robot’s proprioception, and its kinematic model. The harness withholds depth, the camera intrinsics and extrinsics, and perception tools. AMP1 can see the cans in every image, but it has nothing that turns a pixel into a position in the robot’s frame, which it needs before it can plan a grasp.

AMP1 closes this gap by calibrating the wrist camera itself. The wrist camera moves with the gripper, whose pose AMP1 knows at every instant, so images taken at known gripper poses form a multi-view camera rig once two unknowns – the camera’s intrinsics and its fixed pose relative to the gripper – are solved for. The episode succeeded in 44 model calls, of which the calibration and 3D estimation described below took the first 16, all before the first grasp.

Calibration.

AMP1 moved the gripper to a few known poses and kept the wrist image at each (Fig. S6A), then matched SIFT features across the views. It wrote a bundle adjustment routine that performs a least-squares fit of the camera’s intrinsics, its pose relative to the gripper, and the 3D positions of the matched features. The bundle adjustment minimizes the distance between where each point projects and where it was observed. The first fit converged but placed the camera 2.8 m up the tool axis, because shifts and a yaw alone leave the camera’s offset along that axis unobservable. AMP1 diagnosed this, added two views with the tool tilted (Fig. S6B), and re-ran the fit on all seven views. The table plane emerged from the reconstruction without being given, and AMP1 checked the result by projecting the points back onto a view.

Triangulation.

With the camera model, AMP1 located the cans’ top rims (Fig. S7A) and the bin’s rim and the mustard bottle inside it (Fig. S7B) by intersecting rays from several views. The grasps and placements that followed used these positions directly.

S4.2 Active perception

This case study follows one episode of the “Wrist camera only” ablation (Sec. 2D.3, Fig. 5D) on the RoboLab task CubesAndBlocksInBinTask (“Put all the cubes and blocks in the bin”). In this setting, the wrist camera is AMP1’s only view of the scene: its code receives the wrist camera’s RGB and depth images, and there is no scene camera. The task has seven target objects that the arm must pick up and place in the bin: three Rubik’s cubes and a blue, a red, a green, and a yellow block. Because the camera rides on the gripper, it mostly sees only part of the table at a time. At the start, some targets are in view and others are not, so AMP1 first has to work out where to look.

Getting an overview.

At the start pose, AMP1 noted that there might be more objects beyond the edge of the frame and hidden under the gripper (Fig. S8A), so it did not plan from this view. Instead, it lifted the gripper to 0.62 m above the middle of the table to see the whole scene. From there it found the green block and the whole birdhouse. Two problems remained. The bin touched the edge of the image, so its estimated box might be cut short, and objects might lie out of view on the robot’s side of the table. AMP1 therefore moved the camera 0.20 m toward the robot (Fig. S8B). The bin’s box grew from 34 to 42 cm, and the yellow block appeared next to a lizard figurine.

Taking a closer look.

The overviews found every target but measured them poorly. The depth captured mostly the tops of the objects from that height, so two of the Rubik’s cubes and the blue block came out about 2 cm tall instead of about 5 cm. The agent reasoned that perception from that height was too coarse and decided to hover low over each object and look again before grasping it. At the first close look, the Rubik’s cube nearest the robot measured 6.1×\times6.1×\times5.3 cm, with its faces at −51.6-51.6° rather than the 69.9° the overview had given. AMP1 then used the new angle to choose how to close its fingers so that the gripper would not touch the blue block beside the cube (Fig. S8C). For every later pick, AMP1 started with a close look like this one.

S5 Robustness to instruction phrasing on RoboLab-120

RoboLab-120 evaluates every task under three natural-language instruction conditions: default (standard task phrasing), vague (underspecified phrasing that omits explicit object names or attributes), and specific (detailed phrasing that names target objects and relations explicitly) [22]. Fig. S9 compares all 19 policies for which evaluation data exist across all three conditions: seven AMP1 configurations (Gemini 4 Argon, Opus 5.5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Opus 4.5) and 12 baseline policies (11 leaderboard entries plus our evaluation of FLUX 3 Action [23] on the vague and specific conditions, 1,200 trials per condition). For each policy, we report the absolute success rate under default instructions, the absolute spread across the three conditions (max−min\max-\min, in percentage points), and the relative spread (spread/default success rate\text{spread}/\text{default success rate}), and rank all policies from lowest to highest relative spread. Across all seven models, AMP1’s absolute spread stays between 0.9 and 4.5 percentage points, corresponding to a relative spread of 1.9% to 6.4% – occupying the top six positions and seven of the top eight. AMP1 with six models (Opus 5, Opus 4.5, Gemini 4 Argon, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Haiku 5.5) achieves the six lowest relative spreads on the benchmark (1.9%, 2.6%, 3.6%, 3.6%, 5.5%, and 5.8%, respectively). Even with smaller or older models such as Haiku 5.5 (51.6% default success) and Opus 4.5 (35.2% default success), AMP1 maintains relative spreads of 5.8% and 2.6%, lower than every learned policy. Only one learned policy, BiMind v0.5 (6.1%), has a lower relative spread than any AMP1 configuration: AMP1 with Sonnet 5.5 (6.4%), a gap of 0.3 points. By contrast, end-to-end VLA and WAM/LWM baselines exhibit a median relative spread of 42.0%, ranging from 6.1% for BiMind v0.5 to 70.6% for paligemma-binning, with large drops under vague phrasing – including 12.8 percentage points for π0.5\pi_{0.5} [24] (46.1% relative spread), 14.5 percentage points for FLUX 3 Action [23] (33.8%), and 16.2 percentage points for Cosmos3-Nano-Policy (51.9%).

S6 RoboLab-120 failure mode analysis

We examined every failed episode of the two strongest models in the RoboLab-120 evaluation of Fig. 2B, under the ‘default’ instruction condition (10 trials per task, 1,200 trials per model): 173 failed episodes for AMP1 with Gemini 4 Argon (1,027 successes, or 85.6%) and 206 for AMP1 with Opus 5.5 (994 successes, or 82.8%). For each failed episode, we compared the final scene with RoboLab’s programmed verifier and analyzed the agent’s execution trace and measurements, the task verification code, and the final camera frames.

Fig. S10 partitions all 1,200 trials of each model by outcome. It first separates failures by their source – the benchmark (Eval failure), the policy (AMP1 failure), or the model API (Provider failure) – and then breaks each source into specific causes. AMP1 succeeds in every trial of 76 of the 120 tasks with Gemini 4 Argon (66 tasks with Opus 5.5). For both models, roughly two-thirds of the failures stem from the benchmark rather than the policy: 121 of the 173 failures with Gemini 4 Argon (70%), across 25 tasks, and 135 of the 206 failures with Opus 5.5 (66%), across 30 tasks. These benchmark artifacts comprise objects whose width or mass distribution is incompatible with a standard parallel-jaw grasp (77 episodes for Gemini 4 Argon and 101 for Opus 5.5) and flaky verifiers that reject end states that satisfy the instruction (44 and 34 episodes, respectively). Genuine AMP1 failures on graspable objects account for 47 episodes with Gemini 4 Argon (3.9% of all trials) and 71 with Opus 5.5 (5.9%); the remaining 5 episodes with Gemini 4 Argon are terminated by the provider’s safety filter.

Eval failure: Object defect (77 episodes for Gemini 4 Argon, 101 for Opus 5.5).

In 16 tasks for Gemini 4 Argon and 22 tasks for Opus 5.5 (24 distinct tasks in total; Fig. S10), the target object is incompatible with a standard parallel-jaw grasp. Some objects, such as the pomegranate (115 mm), the bagels (100 mm), and the coffee can (102 mm), are wider than the 85-mm maximum aperture of the Robotiq 2F-85 gripper. Others slip out of a friction grasp because of their mass distribution or thin profile, including the 1.5-kg cordless drill, heavy-headed hammers extracted from a bin, a 2-cm-thick flat block, and a moka pot. Only one task fails every trial for both models because of a defect: in FoodPackingByColor, the instruction asks for “the blue object” although the scene contains two, and RoboLab’s verifier accepts only the 102-mm coffee can. In all 10 trials, AMP1 packs the graspable blue SPAM can and fails to hold the oversize coffee can. In the remaining tasks, AMP1 succeeds when it improvises a non-standard grasp (Sec. 2B). For objects wider than the gripper, it holds a narrower feature or supports the object from below: it inserts one finger through the hole of a bagel (BagelsOnPlate and GrabABagel), and it pinches the pomegranate’s narrow crown or pins the fruit against a heavier object and scoops it up with the open gripper (FruitsOnPlate and ClearOrganicObjects; Fig. 3D). For the heavy drill, it replaces the friction grasp with an interlocking one, closing the fingers around the top of the handle so that the head rests on them once the drill is lifted (PickDrill and ToolsPickingDrill; Fig. S4C). Across the 16 affected tasks (160 trials), AMP1 with Gemini 4 Argon still succeeds in 66 episodes (41%); it fails in 77 because of the object defect and in 17 for other reasons (5 flaky-verifier rejections, 8 AMP1 errors, and 4 provider blocks). Across the 22 tasks affected for AMP1 with Opus 5.5 (220 trials), it succeeds in 107 episodes (49%).

Eval failure: Flaky verifier (44 episodes for Gemini 4 Argon, 34 for Opus 5.5).

In 13 tasks for Gemini 4 Argon and 9 tasks for Opus 5.5 (Fig. S10), RoboLab’s verifier rejects end states that satisfy the natural-language instruction. Only one task fails every trial for both models: in RecycleCartonsOnBox (“Put the cartons that can be recycled on the box”), the verifier tests whether the cartons lie inside the box, which is closed, whereas the task’s own progress tracker checks whether they rest on top of it. In all 10 trials for both models, AMP1 places both cartons on top of the box, the progress tracker scores them as placed, and the verifier rejects the outcome. In the remaining tasks, the verifier is overly strict rather than impossible to satisfy: it accepts only a narrow subset of valid placements, so AMP1 still succeeds in 59 of the 130 trials across the 13 tasks with Gemini 4 Argon and in 48 of the 90 trials across the 9 tasks with Opus 5.5. In CookingPickPastaTool (9 verifier rejections for Gemini 4 Argon and 7 for Opus 5.5), the pasta tool ends standing inside the target holder, but the verifier – which requires the tool’s center to lie inside the holder while the tool touches it – does not register it; the single Gemini 4 Argon success came when the episode ended with the gripper still holding the tool inside the holder. In PickUpBluePitcher (6 and 5 rejections), AMP1 lifts the pitcher 8.5 to 12.8 cm above the table, but the verifier’s 5-cm lift check does not trigger. In StackWhiteMugs (5 rejections for Gemini 4 Argon), the verifier rejects deeply nested mugs whose upper bounding-box corners dip below the lower mug’s base; in PickOrangeObject (5 for Opus 5.5), it rejects lifts that sit on the boundary of its height threshold. In MoveBananaToBagelPlate (5 rejections for Gemini 4 Argon), AMP1 places the banana on top of the bagels already on the plate, whereas the verifier requires direct contact with the plate surface. The remaining rejections (9 across 8 tasks for Gemini 4 Argon and 7 across 5 tasks for Opus 5.5) are isolated cases of one or two episodes in which a lifted object or an in-container placement sits just outside the verifier’s geometric threshold, as in PickDrill, GrabABagel, UtensilsInMug, and ToolsPickingAllHammers. In nearly all of these episodes, AMP1 ended the trial believing it had succeeded.

AMP1 failures and provider blocks (52 episodes for Gemini 4 Argon, 71 for Opus 5.5).

The remaining failures are execution or interpretation errors by AMP1 on objects that the gripper can hold with a standard grasp: 47 episodes across 24 tasks for Gemini 4 Argon and 71 episodes across 33 tasks for Opus 5.5 (Fig. S10).

  • •

    Timeout (15 episodes for Gemini 4 Argon, 28 for Opus 5.5): AMP1 exhausts the step budget, or ends the episode itself because too few steps remain to finish the remaining objects. Most timeouts follow earlier setbacks that AMP1 recovers from – repeated regrasps after slips, freeing a wedged finger, or searching for a reachable arm configuration on a shelf – but that consume most of the step budget before the last object is placed.

  • •

    Target dropped (13 for Gemini 4 Argon, 19 for Opus 5.5): A graspable object slips, drops, or tips out of a valid goal state during transport or release, and AMP1 does not recover it before the episode ends.

  • •

    Collision (9 and 11 episodes): The arm, the gripper, or the held object collides with the scene, such as an unperceived upper shelf tier or a bin wall, or knocks a previously placed object out of position.

  • •

    Instruction misread (4 for Gemini 4 Argon, 9 for Opus 5.5): AMP1 identifies the objects in the scene correctly but interprets the instruction too narrowly or too broadly. In SpoonsInPot (4 episodes for Gemini 4 Argon and 7 for Opus 5.5) and GreenSpoonsInPot (1 for Opus 5.5), it takes a deep green utensil with a bent neck for a soup ladle rather than a serving spoon and leaves it out (in one trial actively removing it from the pot), whereas RoboLab’s verifier requires it in the pot. In one trial of OneBottleInSquarePail, Opus 5.5 puts a white-capped utility jug into the pail instead of one of the small white plastic bottles.

  • •

    Gripper not released (3 for Gemini 4 Argon, 4 for Opus 5.5): The object reaches the goal region, but the gripper fails to open or detach cleanly, for example when a bowl rim or a mug handle wedges on the finger linkage, and remains in contact at the end of the episode.

  • •

    Misperception (3 for Gemini 4 Argon, 0 for Opus 5.5): AMP1 misidentifies an object’s category or geometry from the camera images. In two trials of SpoonsInPot, Gemini 4 Argon takes an oval green serving spoon, partly hidden beneath the ladle, for a flat spatula and leaves it on the plate; in one trial of FoodPacking1Boxes, it mistakes a crease on top of a cracker box for the box’s edge and misplaces the grasp.

Finally, 5 episodes with Gemini 4 Argon (Provider failure: Safety filter block) end early because the Gemini API blocks a model request under its safety filter, even after automatic retries; no such blocks occur with Opus 5.5.

Summary.

On the tasks free of both flaky verifiers and object defects, AMP1 succeeds in 96.2% of episodes with Gemini 4 Argon (914 of 950 trials across 95 tasks) and in 93.6% with Opus 5.5 (842 of 900 trials across 90 tasks). On the 84 tasks free of both issues for both models, the success rates are 96.2% and 93.7%, respectively. Without excluding any task, crediting the verifier rejections whose end state satisfies the instruction (44 for Gemini 4 Argon and 34 for Opus 5.5) raises AMP1’s success rate across all 1,200 trials from 85.6% to 89.3% with Gemini 4 Argon and from 82.8% to 85.7% with Opus 5.5.

S7 Inference cost of AMP1

This section estimates the inference cost of AMP1 for the models with public API pricing, the Claude models and Gemini 4 Argon, by pricing each episode’s tokens at list price (Tab. S3). With Opus 5.5, a RoboLab-120 episode costs $1.39 on average, about 26 times lower than the $36.40 reported for Astranomy with GPT-6 Astra [21]. (AMP1 also succeeds more often, 82.8% against 74.8%.) Astranomy queries the model for every small end-effector step, whereas a single AMP1 turn can command a whole trajectory through code, and images enter the model’s context only when it asks for them.

Cost per episode is widely reported, but it mixes two factors: the tokens an episode consumes, which the model and harness determine, and the price per token, which the provider sets. Prices do not track capability. Opus 5 is billed at 25% more than Opus 5.5 for input and output tokens and 2.5 times more for cache reads (Tab. S3). Prices also fall quickly: the cost of a given capability level has dropped by roughly an order of magnitude per year [26, 27]. We therefore report model calls and token counts alongside cost (Fig. S11); unlike cost, they compare models and harnesses independently of the price list.

Reasoning.

More reasoning raises the success rate of every model in Fig. S11A, but it also substantially raises the cost per episode. The extra cost has two sources: the model writes more in each turn, and it takes more turns, each of which re-reads the episode (Fig. S11B, C). How much the extra cost buys depends on the model. For Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, more reasoning adds 14.6 and 17.2 points for about $0.90 more per episode. For Gemini 4 Argon, which has little headroom, it adds 2.3 points for $1.30 more, more than doubling the cost.

Harness.

For the weaker models (Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Opus 4.5), the assistive harness is both more successful and cheaper than the basic harness; for the stronger models (Gemini 4 Argon, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Opus 5), it is less successful at about the same cost (Fig. S11D; see Sec. 2D.2). The weaker models take fewer turns, as the assistive routines replace much of their trial and error, and require fewer tokens (Fig. S11E, F). Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.5 take about 30% fewer turns and cost 36 to 39% less per episode; Haiku 5.5 costs about 10% less. The stronger models take about as many turns as with the basic harness and generate 7 to 10% fewer tokens, but they read 10 to 19% more input, so their cost rises by up to 7%.
